newsitem.title: POLAND: Poland moves to save jobs at Gdansk shipyard.
newsitem.headline: Poland moves to save jobs at Gdansk shipyard.

text.p: The failed Gdansk shipyard was thrown a lifeline on Monday when Poland's Prime Minister Wlodzimierz Cimoszewicz and the firm's receiver announced a plan to save some jobs and continue building ships at the yard.

The yard's receiver, Andrzej Wiercinski, said the bankrupt firm would either be sold to a strategic investor this year or, as envisaged by the prime minister's plan, Gdansk's facilities would be used by the successful Szczecin shipyard to build ships for the Polish merchant fleet.

"One of these options has to be carried out, which means ships will still be built in that particular place in Gdansk," Wiercinski told reporters after meeting Cimoszewicz and Finance Minister Marek Belka.

The Gdansk shipyard -- birthplace of Solidarity, the former Soviet bloc's first free trade union 17 years ago -- has operated under bankruptcy regulations since August last year, when its debts reached more than 415 million zlotys ($138 million).
The company faced final collapse earlier this month when its receiver began dismissing its last 3,800 workers.

The dismissals prompted violent protests by the Solidarity union, which accuses the ex-communist led government of denying aid to the yard because of the trade union's strong links with the opposition.
Solidarity leads a right-leaning electoral bloc that is challenging the ex-communist party in this year's parliamentary polls.

Union members, who burned tyres on streets and clashed with police during anti-government marches last week, scaled down their protest on Monday but warned it could erupt afresh unless concrete steps to save the yard were taken.
The dismissals, in which the first 1,200 people have already lost their jobs, would be the biggest collective lay-off after Poland launched free market reforms eight years ago.

But Wiercinski said about 800 workers could soon find jobs in the yard because the state-owned bank Pekao SA had agreed to extend a loan of more than $10 million to enable the company to finish the construction of one large ship.
Cimoszewicz said that the receiver, who invited bids for the yard's assets in Monday's newspapers, should know within five weeks whether an investor wanted to buy the firm.

If no investor is found, the Szczecin shipyard was likely to set up a new subsidiary using the Gdansk yard's assets to build five ships for the PZM company, for which the government would offer partial credit guarantees, he said.
He added the PZM could order another five ships, if the terms of the first contract were met. Wiercinski also said the strategic investor in the shipyard could count on the PZM orders.
